topics.title: Review of Number Line Representation
topics.concept:
What is a Number Line?

A number line is a straight line with numbers placed at equal intervals. It helps us visualize the order and relationships between different types of numbers.

Types of Numbers on the Number Line:

Number TypeDefinitionExamplesPosition on Number Line
**Whole Numbers**Natural numbers including 00, 1, 2, 3, ...Zero at center, all others right
**Integers**Whole numbers and their negatives..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...Both left (negative) and right (positive) of zero
**Rational Numbers**Numbers that can be expressed as p/q where q ≠ 01/2, -3/4, 2.5, 0.333...Between integers also, infinitely dense

Important Properties:

  • Every point on the number line represents a real number
  • Between any two distinct rational numbers, there are infinitely more rational numbers
  • The number line extends infinitely in both directions

sections.content:
What is a Number Line? A number line is a straight line with numbers placed at equal intervals. It helps us visualize the order and relationships between different types of numbers.

Types of Numbers on the Number Line:

Number TypeDefinitionExamplesPosition on Number Line
Natural NumbersCounting numbers starting from 11, 2, 3, 4, ...Right of zero, equally spaced
Whole NumbersNatural numbers including 00, 1, 2, 3, ...Zero at center, all others right
IntegersWhole numbers and their negatives..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...Both left (negative) and right (positive) of zero
Rational NumbersNumbers that can be expressed as p/q where q ≠ 01/2, -3/4, 2.5, 0.333...Between integers also, infinitely dense

Important Properties: - Every point on the number line represents a real number - Between any two distinct rational numbers, there are infinitely more rational numbers - The number line extends infinitely in both directions

NUMBER LINE SHOWING DIFFERENT NUMBER SETS:

    Natural Numbers (N):       1   2   3   4   5
                                ↓   ↓   ↓   ↓   ↓
    <----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|---->
        -3   -2   -1    0    1    2    3    4    5
    
    Whole Numbers (W):         0   1   2   3   4   5
    Integers (Z):            -3  -2  -1   0   1   2   3


RATIONAL NUMBERS ON NUMBER LINE (Between Integers):

    Locating 2/3 between 0 and 1:
    
    <----|----|----|----|----|----|----|---->
         0    1/3  2/3   1    4/3   5/3   2
    
              ↑
         2/3 is exactly 2/3 of the distance from 0 to 1


LOCATING -3/4 ON NUMBER LINE:

    Step 1: Find -3/4 is between -1 and 0
    Step 2: Divide segment into 4 equal parts
    Step 3: Count 3 parts left from 0
    
    <----|----|----|----|----|----|----|---->
        -1  -3/4 -1/2 -1/4  0    1/4  1/2  3/4
    
              ↑
            -3/4

points: Natural numbers (1,2,3...) are positive integers
Whole numbers include zero (0,1,2,3...)
Integers include negative numbers (...-2,-1,0,1,2...)
Rational numbers fill the gaps between integers on the number line
Every rational number can be plotted exactly on the number line
The set of rational numbers is dense: between any two rationals, there are infinitely more

topics.title: Rational Numbers as Recurring/Terminating Decimals
topics.concept:
What are Terminating and Recurring Decimals?

When we convert a rational number (p/q) to decimal form by dividing p by q, we get either:

Terminating Decimals: The division ends after a finite number of steps.

  • Example: 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75, 7/8 = 0.875
  • Occurs when denominator (in simplest form) has only prime factors 2 and 5

Recurring (Repeating) Decimals: The division never ends; a digit or block of digits repeats forever.

  • Example: 1/3 = 0.333..., 2/7 = 0.285714285714...
  • Represented with a bar: 0.3̅, 0.285714̅

Why Do Recurring Decimals Occur?

When denominator has prime factors other than 2 and 5 (like 3, 7, 11, etc.), the decimal repeats.

sections.content:
What are Terminating and Recurring Decimals?

When we convert a rational number (p/q) to decimal form by dividing p by q, we get either:

Terminating Decimals: The division ends after a finite number of steps. - Example: 1/2 = 0.5, 3/4 = 0.75, 7/8 = 0.875 - Occurs when denominator (in simplest form) has only prime factors 2 and 5

Recurring (Repeating) Decimals: The division never ends; a digit or block of digits repeats forever. - Example: 1/3 = 0.333..., 2/7 = 0.285714285714... - Represented with a bar: 0.3̅, 0.285714̅

Why Do Recurring Decimals Occur? When denominator has prime factors other than 2 and 5 (like 3, 7, 11, etc.), the decimal repeats.

CLASSIFYING RATIONAL NUMBERS:

                        RATIONAL NUMBER (p/q)
                               │
                ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                │                              │
        TERMINATING DECIMAL            RECURRING DECIMAL
        (denominator = 2ᵃ × 5ᵇ)       (denominator has other primes)
                │                              │
     ┌──────────┼──────────┐          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
     │          │          │          │         │         │
   0.5        0.25       0.125      0.3̅      0.142857̅   0.16̅
   (1/2)      (1/4)      (1/8)      (1/3)      (1/7)     (1/6)


CONVERSION PROCESS:

    Terminating Decimal → Fraction:
    0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4
    
    Recurring Decimal → Fraction (method):
    0.3̅ = x
    10x = 3.3̅
    10x - x = 3.3̅ - 0.3̅
    9x = 3
    x = 3/9 = 1/3


LONG DIVISION PATTERNS:

    1 ÷ 3 = 0.333...        1 ÷ 6 = 0.1666...
    3)1.000                   6)1.00000
       0                        0
      10                       10
       9                        6
       --                       40
       10                       36
        9                       --
        10                       4 ←

points: Terminating decimals: denominator has only 2 and 5 as prime factors
Recurring decimals: denominator has at least one prime factor other than 2 or 5
Bar notation (̅) is used to show the repeating block of digits
Every rational number can be expressed as either a terminating or recurring decimal
The converse is also true: every terminating or recurring decimal is a rational number
The length of the repeating block is always less than the denominator

topics.title: Operations on Real Numbers
topics.concept:
What are Real Numbers?

Real numbers include all rational numbers (integers, fractions, terminating/recurring decimals) AND irrational numbers (non-repeating, non-terminating decimals like √2, π).

Operations on Real Numbers:

Real numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero). This means when you perform these operations on real numbers, the result is also a real number.

Key Properties:

PropertyDescriptionExample
**Associative**(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)(2 + √2) + √3 = 2 + (√2 + √3)
**Distributive**a(b + c) = ab + ac√2(3 + √5) = 3√2 + √10
**Identity**a + 0 = a; a × 1 = a√7 + 0 = √7
**Inverse**a + (-a) = 0; a × (1/a) = 1 (a ≠ 0)√5 × (1/√5) = 1

Rational vs Irrational Results:

  • Rational + Rational = Rational
  • Rational + Irrational = Irrational
  • Irrational + Irrational = Can be Rational or Irrational (e.g., √2 + (-√2) = 0 rational)
  • Similar rules apply for multiplication and division

Operations on Real Numbers:

Real numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (except by zero). This means when you perform these operations on real numbers, the result is also a real number.

Key Properties:

PropertyDescriptionExample
Commutativea + b = b + a; a × b = b × a5 + √3 = √3 + 5
Associative(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)(2 + √2) + √3 = 2 + (√2 + √3)
Distributivea(b + c) = ab + ac√2(3 + √5) = 3√2 + √10

points: Real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers
Operations on real numbers follow commutative, associative, and distributive properties
Sum/difference of two irrationals may be rational if they cancel
Product of two irrationals may be rational (e.g., √2 × √2 = 2)
When adding/subtracting radicals, combine only like terms (same radicand)
√a × √b = √(ab) for positive a, b

topics.title: Irrational Numbers and Their Representation
topics.concept:
What are Irrational Numbers?

Irrational numbers are real numbers that cannot be expressed as p/q (where p and q are integers, q ≠ 0). Their decimal expansions are non-terminating and non-repeating.

Examples of Irrational Numbers:

  • √2, √3, √5, √7, ... (square roots of non-perfect squares)
  • π (3.1415926535...)
  • e (2.718281828...)
  • Golden ratio φ (1.618033...)

Proving √2 is Irrational (Classic Proof):

  1. Assume √2 = p/q in simplest form (p, q coprime integers)
  2. Square both sides: 2 = p²/q² → p² = 2q²
  3. This means p² is even → p is even → p = 2k
  4. Substitute: (2k)² = 2q² → 4k² = 2q² → q² = 2k²
  5. This means q² is even → q is even
  6. But then p and q are both even → contradicting "simplest form"
  7. Therefore, √2 cannot be rational

Locating √2 on the Number Line:

Construct a right triangle with legs of length 1. The hypotenuse = √2.

sections.content:
What are Irrational Numbers? Irrational numbers are real numbers that cannot be expressed as p/q (where p and q are integers, q ≠ 0). Their decimal expansions are non-terminating and non-repeating.

Examples of Irrational Numbers: - √2, √3, √5, √7, ... (square roots of non-perfect squares) - π (3.1415926535...) - e (2.718281828...) - Golden ratio φ (1.618033...)

Proving √2 is Irrational (Classic Proof): 1. Assume √2 = p/q in simplest form (p, q coprime integers) 2. Square both sides: 2 = p²/q² → p² = 2q² 3. This means p² is even → p is even → p = 2k 4. Substitute: (2k)² = 2q² → 4k² = 2q² → q² = 2k² 5. This means q² is even → q is even 6. But then p and q are both even → contradicting "simplest form" 7. Therefore, √2 cannot be rational

Locating √2 on the Number Line: Construct a right triangle with legs of length 1. The hypotenuse = √2.

CONSTRUCTING √2 ON NUMBER LINE:

    Step 1: Draw a right triangle with legs = 1 unit
    
                 C
                 |\
                 | \
                 |  \
                 |   \
                 |    \
               1 |     \ √2
                 |      \
                 |       \
                 |        \
            A____|_________B
                   1
    
    Step 2: Using compass, transfer length √2 to number line
    
    <----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|---->
         0    1    √2   2    3    4
    
    √2 ≈ 1.41421356...


CONSTRUCTING √3 ON NUMBER LINE:

    Step 1: Construct √2 first (as above)
    Step 2: Draw perpendicular of length 1 at √2 point
    Step 3: Hypotenuse = √[(√2)² + 1²] = √(2 + 1) = √3
    
                 D
                 |\
                 | \
                 |  \ √3
               1 |   \
                 |    \
            C____|_____E
               √2
    
    Transfer to number line:
    
    <----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|---->
         0    1    √2   2    √3    3    4


APPROXIMATING IRRATIONAL NUMBERS:

    Number    Decimal Approximation    Type
    ──────────────────────────────────────────

points: Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q where p, q are integers
Their decimal expansions are non-terminating and non-repeating
√n is irrational unless n is a perfect square
Irrational numbers can be represented on the number line using geometric constructions
The sum/difference of a rational and irrational is always irrational
The product of a non-zero rational and irrational is always irrational

topics.title: Rationalization of Real Numbers
topics.concept:
What is Rationalization?

Rationalization is the process of eliminating irrational numbers (like √2, √3) from the denominator of a fraction. This makes expressions easier to work with and compare.

Why Rationalize?

  • To simplify expressions
  • To add/subtract fractions with irrational denominators
  • To compare numbers easily
  • Standard form in mathematics often requires rationalized denominators

Methods for Rationalization:

Type of DenominatorMultiply Numerator & Denominator byResult
a + √ba - √b (conjugate)Denominator becomes a² - b
√a + √b√a - √b (conjugate)Denominator becomes a - b

The Conjugate Trick:

The conjugate of (a + √b) is (a - √b). Their product:

(a + √b)(a - √b) = a² - (√b)² = a² - b (a rational number)

sections.content:
What is Rationalization? Rationalization is the process of eliminating irrational numbers (like √2, √3) from the denominator of a fraction. This makes expressions easier to work with and compare.

Why Rationalize? - To simplify expressions - To add/subtract fractions with irrational denominators - To compare numbers easily - Standard form in mathematics often requires rationalized denominators

Methods for Rationalization:

Type of DenominatorMultiply Numerator & Denominator byResult
√a√aDenominator becomes a
a + √ba - √b (conjugate)Denominator becomes a² - b
√a + √b√a - √b (conjugate)Denominator becomes a - b

The Conjugate Trick: The conjugate of (a + √b) is (a - √b). Their product: (a + √b)(a - √b) = a² - (√b)² = a² - b (a rational number)

RATIONALIZATION FLOWCHART:

    START WITH:         1
                       ─────
                       √2
    
         STEP 1: Multiply numerator and denominator by √2
    
                   1 × √2       √2
                 ───────── =   ───
                   √2 × √2       2
    
         RESULT: Denominator is now rational (2)


RATIONALIZING BINOMIAL DENOMINATORS:

    Example:       1
                ───────
                √3 + √2
    
         Conjugate = √3 - √2
    
         Multiply:
         
         1 × (√3 - √2)         √3 - √2
         ──────────────   =   ────────
         (√3 + √2)(√3 - √2)    3 - 2
         
         = √3 - √2


COMPARING BEFORE AND AFTER:

    Before Rationalization:        After Rationalization:
        1                               √2
        ─ ≈ 0.7071                       ─ ≈ 0.7071
        √2                               2
    
    Both are equal, but denominator is now rational!


REAL-WORLD APPLICATION:

    In engineering and physics, rationalization helps in:
    • Calculating impedances in AC circuits
    • Simplifying optics formulas (Snell's law)
    • Computing distances in coordinate geometry

points: Rationalization removes radicals from the denominator
For a single radical √a, multiply by √a/√a
For binomial (a + √b), multiply by conjugate (a - √b)/(a - √b)
The conjugate product always yields a rational number
Rationalization does not change the value of the expression
Always simplify the final answer when possible

topics.title: Laws of Exponents for Real Numbers
topics.concept:
What are the Laws of Exponents?

Exponents (or powers) provide a shorthand way to represent repeated multiplication. These laws work for real numbers as well.

Laws of Exponents (For Real Numbers a, b > 0, and rational exponents):

LawFormulaExample
Quotient Lawaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (m > n)5⁶ ÷ 5² = 5⁴
Power Law(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(3²)⁴ = 3⁸
Power of Product(ab)ᵐ = aᵐ × bᵐ(2×3)⁴ = 2⁴ × 3⁴
Power of Quotient(a/b)ᵐ = aᵐ/bᵐ(4/5)³ = 4³/5³
Zero Exponenta⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0)7⁰ = 1
Negative Exponenta⁻ᵐ = 1/aᵐ (a ≠ 0)2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8
Fractional Exponentaᵐ/ⁿ = ⁿ√(aᵐ) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ8²/³ = ∛(8²) = ∛64 = 4

Important Notes:

  • These laws apply for all real numbers when the expressions are defined
  • For negative bases, careful with even/odd roots
  • 0⁰ is undefined

sections.content:
What are the Laws of Exponents? Exponents (or powers) provide a shorthand way to represent repeated multiplication. These laws work for real numbers as well.

Laws of Exponents (For Real Numbers a, b > 0, and rational exponents):

LawFormulaExample
Product Lawaᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷
Quotient Lawaᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (m > n)5⁶ ÷ 5² = 5⁴
Power Law(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ(3²)⁴ = 3⁸
Power of Product(ab)ᵐ = aᵐ × bᵐ(2×3)⁴ = 2⁴ × 3⁴
Power of Quotient(a/b)ᵐ = aᵐ/bᵐ(4/5)³ = 4³/5³
Zero Exponenta⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0)7⁰ = 1
Negative Exponenta⁻ᵐ = 1/aᵐ (a ≠ 0)2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8
Fractional Exponentaᵐ/ⁿ = ⁿ√(aᵐ) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ8²/³ = ∛(8²) = ∛64 = 4

Important Notes: - These laws apply for all real numbers when the expressions are defined - For negative bases, careful with even/odd roots - 0⁰ is undefined

VISUALIZING EXPONENT LAWS:

    PRODUCT LAW (aᵐ × aⁿ):
    
    2³ × 2² = (2×2×2) × (2×2) = 2⁵
    
    [■■■] × [■■] = [■■■■■]
     3        2         5


    POWER LAW [(aᵐ)ⁿ]:
    
    (2³)² = (2×2×2)² = (8)² = 64 = 2⁶
    
    [■■■]² = [■■■■■■]
        3 → 6


    FRACTIONAL EXPONENT (aᵐ/ⁿ):
    
    8²/³ = (∛8)² = 2² = 4
    
    Step 1: ∛8 = 2 (cube root)
    Step 2: 2² = 4
    
    OR: 8²/³ = ∛(8²) = ∛64 = 4


SCIENTIFIC NOTATION APPLICATION:

    Large numbers: 3.2 × 10⁸ = 320,000,000
    Small numbers: 4.7 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.000047


SIMPLIFYING WITH EXPONENTS:

    Expression:    2⁵ × 3⁵ × 4⁵
                  ───────────
                      6⁵
    
    = (2×3×4)⁵ / 6⁵
    = (24)⁵ / 6⁵
    = (24/6)⁵ = 4⁵
    = 1024

points: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (add exponents when multiplying same base)
aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (subtract exponents when dividing same base)
(aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ (multiply exponents when raising power to power)
(ab)ᵐ = aᵐ × bᵐ (distribute exponent over product)
a⁰ = 1 (any non-zero number to zero power)
a⁻ᵐ = 1/aᵐ (negative exponent means reciprocal)
aᵐ/ⁿ = ⁿ√(aᵐ) (fractional exponents represent roots)
These laws apply to all real numbers where defined
